title_guess: Real GDP vs nominal GDP: factor cost, market price, inflation, base year and the GDP deflator

segments.teaches: GDP can be measured at factor cost or at market price (factor cost plus indirect taxes minus subsidies); market price can rise even when factor cost stays flat; India moved to market price in 2015

elements.what: white card with a big ? and a cream question box: which measure better shows whether production is rising?
India silhouette above the GDP label
GDP splits into factor cost and market price; market price formula in blue with indirect taxes underlined yellow
three year rows on light-blue bands: factor cost flat at 15K, market price 18K/20K/25K; market-price column later framed and filled green
large cartoon pointing hand in a suit sleeve sliding in towards factor cost
black up-arrow over indirect taxes
pointer box: the year India switched to market price, with a cluster of coloured ? bubbles

segments.notes: Running numeric table (constant 15K vs rising market price). The pointing hand is a recurring 'look here' device. The ? bubble cluster signals 'why did they switch?'.
segments.idea: GDP at factor cost vs at market price (factor cost + indirect taxes - subsidies); market price can rise while factor cost stays flat; India switched to market price in 2015
segments.shown_as: a question card asks which measure shows production better; an India silhouette heads GDP, which splits into factor cost and market price (formula with indirect taxes underlined); a year table keeps factor cost at 15K while market price climbs 18K/20K/25K; a cartoon pointing hand slides toward factor cost; a pointer gives the switch year with a cluster of ? bubbles
segments.example: factor cost flat at 15K vs market price 18K / 20K / 25K

segments.teaches: the switch matched global practice: major economies use market price, the UN national accounts system recommended it, and it makes India's growth comparable

elements.what: world map inside an oval globe outline, India marked
pointer box above the globe: major economies measure at market price
letter-spaced caption under a blue rule: method changed to match global practice
UN flag picture on a white card with a note on its recommendation year
cream box: comparison with developed nations becomes easier

segments.notes: UN emblem must not be reused by BIE.
segments.idea: the switch matched global practice (major economies, the UN accounts system) and makes India's growth comparable
segments.shown_as: a world map in an oval globe with India marked under a pointer saying major economies use market price; a caption on matching global practice, a UN flag card with its recommendation year, and a box on easier comparison

segments.teaches: back to the question: factor cost looks like the better production indicator, but even it can rise without more production

elements.what: ? and GDP / market-price chip shown briefly, then the full question card and table return
green highlighter on 'better indicator' in the question; factor-cost column framed and filled green
grey note under the column: factor-cost GDP rises only when production rises
red cross stamped on that note (it is not quite true)

segments.notes: Set-up and knock-down: a claim is shown, then crossed out to open the next idea (inflation).
segments.idea: factor cost looks like the better production indicator, but even it can rise with no extra production
segments.shown_as: the question card and table return; 'better indicator' is highlighted and the factor-cost column framed green; a note says factor-cost GDP rises only when production rises, and a red cross is stamped on it

segments.teaches: with 10 percent inflation one laptop's factor cost goes 10K -> 11K -> 12.1K, so GDP rises every year though output stays at one laptop: inflated GDP

elements.what: red heading 'inflation' with the rate written beside it
laptop over the factor-cost column
India silhouette over the GDP column
year rows with quantity fixed at 1, factor cost filled row by row (10K, 11K, 12.1K) in white chips
dotted arrows carrying each factor cost into the GDP column
red bracketed label on a row: inflated GDP
cream panel dropped behind the whole table
line under the table: no extra production, yet GDP kept rising

segments.notes: Running numeric example with compounding (10, 11, 12.1). Quantity column fixed at 1 isolates the price effect.
segments.idea: with 10% inflation one laptop's factor cost goes 10K -> 11K -> 12.1K, so GDP rises every year though output stays one laptop: inflated GDP
segments.shown_as: under a red 'inflation 10%' heading, a laptop heads the factor-cost column and an India silhouette the GDP column; quantity stays 1 in every year row while factor cost fills 10K, 11K, 12.1K and dotted arrows carry each into GDP; a row is tagged 'inflated GDP' and a line notes no extra production

segments.teaches: nominal GDP contains an inflation layer; remove it and you get real GDP

elements.what: blue block for GDP with a yellow 'inflation' stripe through the middle
second copy of the block; its yellow stripe slides out to the right and the block closes up
label 'nominal' struck through in red and 'real' written above in green
India silhouette between the two blocks

segments.notes: Physical metaphor: inflation is a removable layer of the bar. Strike-and-replace used on a word, not a number.
segments.idea: nominal GDP holds an inflation layer; take it out and you have real GDP
segments.shown_as: a blue GDP block has a yellow 'inflation' stripe through it; in a second copy the stripe slides out to the right and the block closes up, while 'nominal' is struck in red and 'real' written above in green

segments.teaches: real GDP strips out price rises back to a fixed base year (FY 2012 on screen), not just the previous year

elements.what: thick black year line with ticks for three recent financial years, a laptop and its price over each
dotted curved arcs hopping backwards year to year under the line, then hopping all the way back to the base year
cream box marking the base year on the line

segments.notes: Timeline with backward arcs shows 'remove inflation step by step to the base year'. The blocks from the previous segment stay on top.
segments.idea: real GDP strips price rises all the way back to a fixed base year (FY 2012), not just to last year
segments.shown_as: a thick year line shows three recent years with a laptop and its price over each; dotted arcs hop backwards year to year, then all the way back to a cream-boxed base year
segments.example: laptop prices traced back to base year FY 2012

segments.teaches: real GDP = value at base-year prices; nominal GDP = value at current prices; the tool that converts one to the other is the GDP deflator

elements.what: pink panels: nominal GDP around the latest year (laptop, price), real GDP around the base year
light-blue question card with ?: how to remove inflation from base year to today
condensed heading GDP deflator
syringe drawn beside the deflator heading

segments.notes: Visual metaphor: the deflator as an injection that 'deflates' the number.
segments.idea: real GDP = value at base-year prices; nominal GDP = value at today's prices; the GDP deflator converts one to the other
segments.shown_as: pink panels frame nominal GDP round the latest year (laptop and price) and real GDP round the base year; a question card asks how to remove the inflation, answered by a 'GDP deflator' heading with a syringe drawn beside it

segments.teaches: real GDP = nominal GDP / GDP deflator, worked with the laptop price

elements.what: pink real-GDP panel = pink nominal-GDP panel over a thick fraction bar with the deflator under it = numeric fraction (price over deflator in red) = faded result
question card moved to the top
syringe deflator label under the fraction bar

segments.notes: The panels from the timeline are reused as the terms of the formula, so the equation is built from objects already on screen.
segments.idea: real GDP = nominal GDP / GDP deflator, worked with the laptop price
segments.shown_as: the pink panels become the terms: real GDP = nominal GDP over a thick fraction bar with the syringe deflator under it = price over deflator in red = a faded result

segments.teaches: GDP splits into real (constant prices) and nominal; each can be at factor cost or market price: four ways

elements.what: GDP -> real / nominal with blue arrows, each splitting again into factor cost / market price
pointer box on real GDP: GDP at constant prices
big red '4' over 'ways of calculating' heading

segments.idea: GDP can be real (constant prices) or nominal, each at factor cost or market price: four ways
segments.shown_as: GDP -> real / nominal by blue arrows, each splitting into factor cost / market price, under a big red 4 'ways of calculating' heading, with a pointer 'constant prices' on real

segments.teaches: India headlines nominal GDP at market price; why is the open question for the next video

elements.what: heading moved to top-left: 4 ways of calculating GDP
list of the four combinations
India silhouette next to the last row
pink band on the nominal-at-market-price row
orange Hindi 'why?' word with a ? beside the highlighted row

segments.notes: Tree collapses into a list; ends on a cliff-hanger question in Hinglish.
segments.idea: India headlines nominal GDP at market price; why is left for the next video
segments.shown_as: the tree collapses into a four-line list under the heading; an India silhouette marks the last row, which gets a pink band and an orange Hindi 'why?' with a ?

elements.what: next-video and playlist panels

running_examples: factor cost flat at 15K vs market price 18K / 20K / 25K

best_moments.why: the inflation stripe slides out of the GDP block: real vs nominal as a removable layer
quantity fixed at 1 while value climbs shows inflated GDP
arcs hopping back along the year line to the base year
the formula is built from panels already on screen
